Solar is one of the fastest ways to expand electricity access, particularly in hard-to-reach rural communities. But with many systems such as solar inverters having a lifespan of 15-20 years, how do we ensure that today's clean energy solutions don't become tomorrow's sustainability challenge?
 
That question is becoming increasingly urgent as Africa's clean energy transition gains pace.
Installed renewable energy capacity has doubled over the past decade, from around 35 GW in 2015 to 70 GW in 2024, while 2025 recorded a record 11.3 GW of new renewable capacity additions, led by Ethiopia, South Africa and Egypt. Today, eight African countries generate more than 80% of their electricity from renewable sources.
 
As this momentum continues, the next challenge is ensuring these gains are built to last. Embedding circularity across renewable energy value chains, from critical minerals and manufacturing to repurposing and second-life battery applications, can strengthen energy security, reduce waste, as well as create local industries and jobs.
 
Coming just days after the African Circular Economy Alliance Annual Meeting in Abidjan, I look forward to continuing this important conversation in New York at the UN High-level Political Forum side event, Scaling Circular Renewable Energy Systems: Delivering Inclusive and Resilient Transitions in Africa.
 
Circular energy systems aren't a separate conversation from our global energy systems. They are how we make the clean energy transition more resilient, more sustainable, and more beneficial for communities across Africa, and across the world.
